## Q1. `read.csv` (base R) vs `read_csv` (tidyverse) vs `fread` (data.table)

### Q1.1 Speed, memory, and data types

There are quite a few utilities in R for reading plain text data files. Let us test the speed of reading a moderate sized compressed csv file, `admissions.csv.gz`, by three functions: `read.csv` in base R, `read_csv` in tidyverse, and `fread` in the data.table package.

Which function is fastest? Is there difference in the (default) parsed data types? How much memory does each resultant dataframe or tibble use? (Hint: `system.time` measures run times; `pryr::object_size` measures memory usage.) 

```{r}
system.time(df1 <- read.csv("~/mimic/hosp/admissions.csv.gz"))
system.time(df2 <- read_csv("~/mimic/hosp/admissions.csv.gz"))
system.time(df3 <- fread("~/mimic/hosp/admissions.csv.gz"))
```

As for the default parsed data types, we can use the `str` function to display the structure of the data frame or tibble. 
```{r}
str(df1)
```
```{r}
str(df2)
```
```{r}
str(df3)
```


```{r}
object_size(df1)
object_size(df2)
object_size(df3)
```
**Answer:** 

- As for run time, the fread function is the fastest. 

- The default data types are different for the 3 methods. For example, the `read_csv` function uses the `numeric` data type for the `subject_id` and `hadm_id` columns, while the `read.csv` and `fread` functions use the `integer` data type for the same columns.

- In terms of memory usage, the resultant dataframe of read.csv uses the most memory (158.71 MB). The resultant tibble of read_csv uses 55.31 MB. The resultant data.table of fread uses the least memory (50.13 MB).


### Q1.2 User-supplied data types

Re-ingest `admissions.csv.gz` by indicating appropriate column data types in `read_csv`. Does the run time change? How much memory does the result tibble use? (Hint: `col_types` argument in `read_csv`.)

```{r}
system.time(df4 <- read_csv("~/mimic/hosp/admissions.csv.gz", 
                col_types = cols(subject_id = col_integer(), 
                                 hadm_id = col_integer(),
                                 admission_type = col_factor(),
                                 admission_location = col_factor(),
                                 discharge_location = col_factor(),
                                 insurance = col_factor(),
                                 language = col_factor(),
                                 marital_status = col_factor(),
                                 race = col_factor())))
```

```{r}
object_size(df4)
```
**Answer:**

- The run time is a little bit faster than the default `read_csv` function.

- The resultant tibble of read_csv with user-supplied data types uses 39.79 MB, which is less than the default `read_csv` function.



## Q2. Ingest big data files


### Q2.1 Ingest `labevents.csv.gz` by `read_csv`

<p align="center">
  <img src="./readr_logo.png" width="20%">
</p>

Try to ingest `labevents.csv.gz` using `read_csv`. What happens? If it takes more than 5 minutes on your computer, then abort the program and report your findings. 

```{r}
#| eval: false
lab <- read_csv("~/mimic/hosp/labevents.csv.gz")
```
**Answer:** The `read_csv` function did not finish ingesting `labevents.csv.gz`within 5 minutes. It is because the file is too large, and my computer has limited memory. THe `labevents.csv` file is 13GB, we need at least 26 GB of memory to ingest this file, while my computer only has 16 GB of memory.


### Q2.2 Ingest selected columns of `labevents.csv.gz` by `read_csv`

Try to ingest only columns `subject_id`, `itemid`, `charttime`, and `valuenum` in `labevents.csv.gz` using `read_csv`.  Does this solve the ingestion issue? (Hint: `col_select` argument in `read_csv`.)
```{r}
#| eval: false
lab2 <- read_csv("~/mimic/hosp/labevents.csv.gz", col_select = c(subject_id, itemid, charttime, valuenum))
```
**Answer:** It does not solve the ingestion issue. The `read_csv` function did not finish ingesting the selected columns of `labevents.csv.gz` within 5 minutes and lead to a crash. My computer does not have enough memory to ingest this file.

### Q2.3 Ingest subset of `labevents.csv.gz`

<p align="center">
  <img src="./linux_logo.png" width="20%">
</p>

Our first strategy to handle this big data file is to make a subset of the `labevents` data.  Read the [MIMIC documentation](https://mimic.mit.edu/docs/iv/modules/hosp/labevents/) for the content in data file `labevents.csv`.

In later exercises, we will only be interested in the following lab items: creatinine (50912), potassium (50971), sodium (50983), chloride (50902), bicarbonate (50882), hematocrit (51221), white blood cell count (51301), and glucose (50931) and the following columns: `subject_id`, `itemid`, `charttime`, `valuenum`. Write a Bash command to extract these columns and rows from `labevents.csv.gz` and save the result to a new file `labevents_filtered.csv.gz` in the current working directory. (Hint: use `zcat <` to pipe the output of `labevents.csv.gz` to `awk` and then to `gzip` to compress the output. To save render time, put `#| eval: false` at the beginning of this code chunk.)

Display the first 10 lines of the new file `labevents_filtered.csv.gz`. How many lines are in this new file? How long does it take `read_csv` to ingest `labevents_filtered.csv.gz`? 

```{bash}
#| eval: false
zcat < ~/mimic/hosp/labevents.csv.gz | awk -F, '($5 == 50912 || $5 == 50971 || $5 == 50983 || $5 == 50902 || $5 == 50882 || $5 == 51221 || $5 == 51301 || $5 == 50931) {print $2","$5","$7","$10}' | gzip > labevents_filtered.csv.gz
```

The first 10 lines of the new file `labevents_filtered.csv.gz`:
```{bash}
zcat < labevents_filtered.csv.gz | head -10
```
```{bash}
zcat < labevents_filtered.csv.gz | wc -l
```
```{r}
(time_lab3 <- system.time(lab3 <- read_csv("labevents_filtered.csv.gz")))
```
**Answer:** 

- The `labevents_filtered.csv.gz` file has 24855909 lines.

- The `read_csv` function took `r time_lab3[3]` to ingest the file.

### Q2.4 Ingest `labevents.csv` by Apache Arrow

<p align="center">
  <img src="./arrow_logo.png" width="30%">
</p>

Our second strategy is to use [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/) for larger-than-memory data analytics. Unfortunately Arrow does not work with gz files directly. First decompress `labevents.csv.gz` to `labevents.csv` and put it in the current working directory. To save render time, put `#| eval: false` at the beginning of this code chunk.

Then use [`arrow::open_dataset`](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/reference/open_dataset.html) to ingest `labevents.csv`, select columns, and filter `itemid` as in Q2.3. How long does the ingest+select+filter process take? Display the number of rows and the first 10 rows of the result tibble, and make sure they match those in Q2.3. (Hint: use `dplyr` verbs for selecting columns and filtering rows.)

Write a few sentences to explain what is Apache Arrow. Imagine you want to explain it to a layman in an elevator. 

- Decompress `labevents.csv.gz` to `labevents.csv`:
```{bash}
#| eval: false
gzip -dk < ~/mimic/hosp/labevents.csv.gz > ~/labevents.csv
```

```{r}
(time_lab4 <- system.time(lab4 <- arrow::open_dataset("~/labevents.csv", format = "csv") %>% 
  dplyr::select(subject_id, itemid, charttime, valuenum) %>% 
  # dplyr::filter(itemid == 50912 | itemid == 50971 | itemid == 50983 | itemid == 50902 | itemid == 50882 | itemid == 51221 | itemid == 51301 | itemid == 50931) %>%
  dplyr::filter(itemid %in% c(50912, 50971, 50983, 50902, 50882, 51221, 51301, 50931)) %>% 
  collect()))
```
```{r}
nrow(lab4)
```
```{r}
head(lab4, 10)
```
**Answer:**

-It takes `r time_lab4[3]` seconds to ingest, select, and filter the `labevents.csv` file. 

-The number of rows is 24855909 and the first 10 rows of the result tibble match those in Q2.3.


### Q2.5 Compress `labevents.csv` to Parquet format and ingest/select/filter

<p align="center">
  <img src="./parquet_logo.png" width="30%">
</p>

Re-write the csv file `labevents.csv` in the binary Parquet format (Hint: [`arrow::write_dataset`](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/reference/write_dataset.html).) How large is the Parquet file(s)? How long does the ingest+select+filter process of the Parquet file(s) take? Display the number of rows and the first 10 rows of the result tibble and make sure they match those in Q2.3. (Hint: use `dplyr` verbs for selecting columns and filtering rows.)

Write a few sentences to explain what is the Parquet format. Imagine you want to explain it to a layman in an elevator.

```{r eval=FALSE}
lab_csv <- arrow::open_dataset("~/labevents.csv", format = 'csv')
arrow::write_dataset(lab_csv, "labevents.parquet")
```

```{r}
file.size("~/labevents.csv")
file.size("labevents.parquet/part-0.parquet")
```

```{r}
(time_lab_parquet <- system.time(lab_parquet <- arrow::open_dataset("labevents.parquet/part-0.parquet", format = "parquet") %>% 
  dplyr::select(subject_id, itemid, charttime, valuenum) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(itemid %in% c(50912, 50971, 50983, 50902, 50882, 51221, 51301, 50931)) %>% 
  collect()))
```

```{r}
nrow(lab_parquet)
```
```{r}
head(lab_parquet, 10)
```
**Answer:**

- The `labevents.csv` file is 13.7 GB, while the `labevents.parquet` file is about 2 GB.

- It takes `r time_lab_parquet[3]` seconds to ingest, select, and filter the `labevents.parquet` file, which is faster than the `labevents.csv` file.

- The number of rows is 24855909 and the first 10 rows of the result tibble match those in Q2.3.

-  Parquet is a storage format that arranges data in columns, making it ideal for efficiently managing large datasets during both read and write processes. Its design excels particularly when queries target specific columns of a table, guaranteeing optimal performance for such operations.

### Q2.6 DuckDB

<p align="center">
  <img src="./duckdb_logo.png" width="20%">
</p>

Ingest the Parquet file, convert it to a DuckDB table by     [`arrow::to_duckdb`](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/reference/to_duckdb.html), select columns, and filter rows as in Q2.5. How long does the ingest+convert+select+filter process take? Display the number of rows and the first 10 rows of the result tibble and make sure they match those in Q2.3. (Hint: use `dplyr` verbs for selecting columns and filtering rows.)

Write a few sentences to explain what is DuckDB. Imagine you want to explain it to a layman in an elevator.

```{r}
(time_lab_duckdb <- system.time(
  lab_duckdb <- arrow::open_dataset("labevents.parquet/part-0.parquet", format = "parquet") %>% 
  dplyr::select(subject_id, itemid, charttime, valuenum) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(itemid %in% c(50912, 50971, 50983, 50902, 50882, 51221, 51301, 50931)) %>% 
  arrow::to_duckdb() %>%
  collect()))
```


```{r}
nrow(lab_duckdb)
```
```{r}
head(lab_duckdb, 10)
```
**Answer:**

- It takes `r time_lab_duckdb[3]` seconds to ingest, convert, select, and filter the `labevents.parquet` file to a DuckDB table.

- The number of rows is 24855909 and the first 10 rows of the result tibble match those in Q2.3.

- DuckDB is an embeddable SQL OLAP database management system. It is used as an embedded database, which means it runs as part of the application and does not require a separate server process. It is designed to be fast and efficient for analytical queries, and it is optimized for read-heavy workloads. The system is designed for user-friendly integration with other systems.

## Q3. Ingest and filter `chartevents.csv.gz`

[`chartevents.csv.gz`](https://mimic.mit.edu/docs/iv/modules/icu/chartevents/) contains all the charted data available for a patient. During their ICU stay, the primary repository of a patient’s information is their electronic chart. The `itemid` variable indicates a single measurement type in the database. The `value` variable is the value measured for `itemid`. The first 10 lines of `chartevents.csv.gz` are
```{bash}
zcat < ~/mimic/icu/chartevents.csv.gz | head -10
```
[`d_items.csv.gz`](https://mimic.mit.edu/docs/iv/modules/icu/d_items/) is the dictionary for the `itemid` in `chartevents.csv.gz`.
```{bash}
zcat < ~/mimic/icu/d_items.csv.gz | head -10
```
In later exercises, we are interested in the vitals for ICU patients: heart rate (220045), mean non-invasive blood pressure (220181), systolic non-invasive blood pressure (220179), body temperature in Fahrenheit (223761), and respiratory rate (220210). Retrieve a subset of `chartevents.csv.gz` only containing these items, using the favorite method you learnt in Q2. 

Document the steps and show code. Display the number of rows and the first 10 rows of the result tibble.


- Extract these columns `subject_id`, `itemid`, `charttime`, `valuenum` and rows in the vitals for ICU patients from `chartevents.csv.gz` and save the result to a new file `chartevents_filtered.csv.gz` in the current working directory. 
```{bash}
#| eval: false
zcat < ~/mimic/icu/chartevents.csv.gz | awk -F, '($7 == 220045 || $7 == 220181 || $7 == 220179 || $7 == 223761 || $7 == 220210) {print $1","$5","$7","$9}' | gzip > chartevents_filtered.csv.gz
```

- Display the first 10 lines of the new file `chartevents_filtered.csv.gz`.
```{bash}
zcat < chartevents_filtered.csv.gz | head -10
```
- Display the number of rows in the new file `chartevents_filtered.csv.gz`.
```{bash}
zcat < chartevents_filtered.csv.gz | wc -l
```

- I did not generated the Parquet format in Homework 2. I will generate the Parquet format here, to save some memory, I filtered the useful information from `chartevents.csv.gz` according to the item id and then decompressed `chartevents_filtered_2.csv.gz` to `chartevents_2.csv`. Finally, I used `arrow` to convert `chartevents_2.csv` to Parquet format.

```{bash}
#| eval: false
# Filter useful information from chartevents.csv.gz according to the item id
zcat < ~/mimic/icu/chartevents.csv.gz | awk -F, 'NR == 1 || \
($7 == 220045 || $7 == 220180 || $7 == 220179 || $7 == 223761 || $7 == 220210)\
{print $1","$3","$5","$7","$9}' | gzip > chartevents_filtered_2.csv.gz
```

- Decompress `chartevents_filtered_2.csv.gz` to `chartevents_2.csv`:
```{bash}
#| eval: false
gzip -dk < ./chartevents_filtered_2.csv.gz > ~/chartevents_2.csv
```

```{r eval=FALSE}
chart_csv <- arrow::open_dataset("~/chartevents_2.csv", format = 'csv')
arrow::write_dataset(chart_csv, "chartevents_pq")
```
